questions.q: What problem do managed identities solve?
options: Applications needing to store connection strings or access keys as secrets, which can leak and need rotation
Slow network connections between Azure regions
The cost of running virtual machines
Data being stored in the wrong file format
questions.explain: Managed identities let a resource authenticate without any secret stored in code, config, or source control.

questions.q: What is a system-assigned managed identity?
options: An identity tied to the lifecycle of exactly one resource — created and deleted along with it
An identity that must be manually created and never expires
An identity shared automatically across every resource in a subscription
A synonym for an RBAC role
questions.explain: Delete the resource, and its system-assigned identity is deleted with it.

questions.q: What is a user-assigned managed identity?
options: A standalone Azure resource, independent of any one thing using it, that can be attached to multiple resources needing the same access
An identity that requires a human user to log in every time
The same thing as a system-assigned identity with a different name
An identity that only works with virtual machines
questions.explain: Because it's its own resource, a user-assigned identity can outlive or be shared across whatever uses it.

questions.q: What does a managed identity still need before it can access a storage account?
options: A role assignment (RBAC), exactly like Lesson 5 covered, scoped to what it needs to touch
Nothing else — having a managed identity automatically grants full access to everything
A stored connection string in addition to the identity
A manually typed password
questions.explain: A managed identity is just an identity — it still needs an RBAC role assignment to actually be granted access.

questions.q: Why is a managed identity considered more secure than a stored connection string?
options: There's nothing to leak or rotate manually, and access is auditable through normal Azure AD sign-in and activity logs
Managed identities are encrypted twice, unlike connection strings
Managed identities cannot be used to access storage accounts, only compute resources
There is no security difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: Azure manages the credential lifecycle entirely, removing the biggest risks of manually stored secrets.
